planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this cultivar spreads at roughly the same pace as common Japanese spurge but is grown chiefly for its deeply lobed, lacy foliage rather than speed of cover.

directions: This sport of common Japanese spurge carries the same glossy, dark-green, whorled leaves but each one is deeply incised into narrow, jagged lobes, giving established patches a fine, almost fern-like texture that reads very differently from a standard pachysandra planting from a distance. Plant divisions in consistently moist, humus-rich soil under trees or on north-facing slopes where turf struggles, keeping new plantings watered through their first year while the shallow root system establishes. Small white flower spikes appear in early spring but are secondary to the foliage display; shear back winter-damaged leaves in late winter to refresh the planting before new growth emerges. Its habit and hardiness track the species closely, so use it as a texture accent within a larger pachysandra bed rather than expecting faster coverage.

common_name: Windcliff Fragrant Pachysandra (Dan Hinkley Chinese Spurge Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade to full shade; this selection was collected by plant explorer Dan Hinkley in China and is grown specifically for stronger, more reliable flower fragrance than typical Chinese pachysandra.

directions: Windcliff Fragrant produces spidery white flower spikes tucked among the glossy evergreen leaves in spring, with a distinct, carrying sweetness that stands out from the merely faint scent typical of the species, and it often repeats a light bloom flush again in fall. Grow it in evenly moist, rich, well-drained soil under high shade, siting it where the fragrance can be appreciated near a path or seating area. It spreads by low stolons at a measured, well-mannered pace, forming a spreading low mat rather than an upright clump, so give it room to knit together over a couple of seasons rather than crowding plants tightly. Water during dry spells in the first year or two; once established it needs little beyond an occasional tidy-up of winter-worn foliage in late winter.

common_name: Forest Green Allegheny Spurge (Uniform Native Pachysandra Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Forest Green was selected at Penn State for larger leaf whorls and a cleaner, more uniform carpet than typical seed-grown Allegheny spurge.

directions: Forest Green was picked out decades ago for its larger, shinier, more consistently dark-green leaf whorls, which fill in with noticeably less of the mottled, undulating variation that seed-grown Allegheny spurge typically shows, giving plantings a tidier, more formal appearance. Fragrant white bottlebrush flower spikes emerge at the base of the clump in late winter before new leaves push up, drawing early-season pollinators on mild days. Set divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic soil in dappled to full shade; this is a slow, clump-forming spreader rather than an aggressive runner, so space plants closer than the species if faster coverage is the goal. Provide more shade in southern gardens to prevent leaf scorch, and mulch lightly to conserve moisture through summer heat.

common_name: Little's Pixie Dragon Allegheny Spurge (Dwarf Toothed-Leaf Native Pachysandra)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this Virginia-collected dwarf selection stays noticeably smaller than typical Allegheny spurge and shows off best with its jagged, mottled leaves at eye level along a path edge.

directions: Little's Pixie Dragon stays compact and slow-spreading compared with typical Allegheny spurge, with distinctive silver-mottled leaves whose margins are cut into sharp, saw-like teeth rather than the soft scalloping of the species, giving the foliage a spiky, dragon-scale look up close. Clusters of soft pink flower spikes emerge low on the clump in early spring ahead of the new leaves. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, slightly acidic soil in part to full shade, since direct sun quickly bleaches the mottled leaf pattern; established plants handle short dry spells but perform best with steady moisture. Because it spreads more slowly than seed-grown Allegheny spurge, use it as a refined accent near a path or in a small woodland container rather than a fast-filling bulk groundcover.
